lead: A GIS layer is only useful if its numbers land on the right spot. Latitude and longitude describe a place on a curved earth; easting and northing describe it on a flat grid. A projection converts one to the other, and a datum says which earth the numbers belong to. Every layer must state its datum, projection and units, or features from different sources will not line up. District GIS, cadastral maps and utility networks all depend on this.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for datums and coordinate systems, and 7.3 for how coordinates ride with the geometry.

blocks.text: A position on the earth is a latitude (angle north or south of the equator) and a longitude (angle east or west of the prime meridian), both in degrees measured on an ellipsoid — a smooth mathematical surface close to the real earth. The geoid is a different surface: mean sea level, continued under the land. A datum fixes one chosen ellipsoid to the earth with a stated origin and orientation, so a coordinate names one place and no other. WGS84 is the global datum of GNSS; the Everest ellipsoid, fixed by an older Indian datum, is the basis of Indian topographic sheets.

Degrees do not give flat-plane distance. One degree of longitude is about 111 km at the equator and shrinks to zero at the poles, so geometry in degrees is distorted. A projection turns latitude and longitude into easting and northing in metres on a plane. No projection keeps every property: it can keep shape (conformal), keep area (equal-area), keep one distance, or keep directions from one point. Pick by the job.

sections.h3: Projection families and the UTM grid

blocks.text: Cylindrical projections wrap a cylinder around the earth; conic projections use a cone; azimuthal projections use a plane touching at one point. Transverse Mercator is a cylinder turned sideways, touching along a meridian, so it suits a north-south strip of country.

UTM divides the world into 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide, numbered from zone 1 at 180° W. Zone n runs from 180° + 6(n − 1) to 180° + 6n degrees. So zone number = floor((longitude + 180) ÷ 6) + 1. Each zone has a central meridian. There the scale factor is 0.9996: a 1000 m line on the ground measures 999.6 m on the grid, 0.4 m short per kilometre. A false easting of 500 000 m is added so eastings never go negative; a false northing of 10 000 000 m does the same for northings in the southern hemisphere. India falls roughly in zones 42 to 47.

Software reprojects on the fly, converting a layer into the display projection. That fixes the projection only. A wrong datum still shifts features — hundreds of metres between WGS84 and an old Indian datum. Indian topographic sheets are drawn on the Everest ellipsoid and their margins name the projection, so read the margin rather than assume.

figure.caption: Each level of the stack must be written in the data. A mismatch at the datum level shifts every feature on the map.

examples.question: A point near Chennai is at 80° E, 13° N. Find (a) its UTM zone number, (b) the zone's central meridian, (c) how far west of that meridian the point lies, and (d) the grid length of a 1000 m ground line at the central meridian.
steps: Zone 44 starts at 180 + 6 × 43 = 438°, which is 78° E after removing 360°, and ends at 84° E. Its central meridian is 78° + 3° = 81° E.
The point at 80° E lies 81° − 80° = 1° west of the central meridian.
At the central meridian the scale factor k = 0.9996, so grid length = 1000 m × 0.9996 = 999.6 m. The shortfall is 1000 − 999.6 = 0.4 m in 1 km.
The false easting on the central meridian is 500 000 m, so eastings inside the zone stay positive.
examples.answer: Zone 44, central meridian 81° E, point 1° west of it, and a 1000 m ground line measures 999.6 m on the grid (0.4 m short).
examples.check:
import math
lon = 80.0
zone = math.floor((lon + 180) / 6) + 1
west = -180 + 6 * (zone - 1)
cm = west + 3
grid = 1000 * 0.9996
diff = 1000 - grid
print(int(zone))
print(int(cm))
print(round(grid, 1))
print(round(diff, 1))

traps: Feeding degrees into software that expects metres, or the reverse.
Assuming two layers with the same numeric range share a datum; equal numbers are not equal places.
Believing on-the-fly reprojection repairs a wrong datum. It repairs the projection only.
Choosing a projection before deciding which property — area, shape or distance — the job needs.
Forgetting the false easting and northing, then reading negative eastings or a mirrored southern-hemisphere grid.

quiz.q: Define a datum in one line.
quiz.a: An ellipsoid fixed to the earth with a stated origin and orientation, so coordinates refer to one place.

quiz.q: Why can a GIS not measure distance directly in degrees?
quiz.a: A degree of longitude is about 111 km at the equator and falls to zero at the poles, so degree geometry is not a plane distance.

quiz.q: Find the UTM zone of a point at 77° E.
A 5000 m ground line lies on the central meridian of a UTM zone. What is its grid length?
Two layers share a projection, but features in one sit about 200 m off the other. Diagnosis?
quiz.a: A datum mismatch — for example WGS84 coordinates entered into a layer built on the Everest-based Indian datum. Reprojection will not remove it.

quiz.q: Why is a false easting of 500 000 m added in UTM?
quiz.a: So that eastings inside the 6° zone stay positive and the grid carries no negative signs.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every projection and datum pair is registered by a numeric EPSG code; WGS84 with UTM zone 44N is EPSG:32644, which is why GIS files store a code rather than a name. Survey departments are moving to datum epochs, because plate motion shifts WGS84 coordinates by centimetres every year. Search 'EPSG registry' and 'datum epoch' next.
